spans.assertion: the analysis used data from 146,028 player-referee dyads across European soccer leagues (2012-2013 season)

an exploratory, in-sample analysis was conducted specifically designed to identify the strongest defensible evidence supporting the hypothesis that referees favor giving red cards to dark-skinned players
the analysis was explicitly framed as an exploratory advocacy analysis / red-team stress test to determine the upper bound of in-sample support for the hypothesis

an exhaustive specification search was performed across multiple thresholds, model specifications, and standard-error estimators to maximize supportive evidence while maintaining rigor and transparency

dark-skin-toned players (≥0.75) receive red cards at a significantly higher rate than very-light-skin-toned players (0.00), even after adjusting for position, league, games, and player characteristics
the primary comparison group was defined as very light skin (0.00) vs dark skin (≥0.75)
the adjusted risk difference for dark vs very light skin was 0.37 percentage points, 95% CI [0.08,0.66], two-sided p=0.013, SE=0.15pp
after adjustment, dark-skinned players have a 0.37 percentage-point higher probability of receiving a red card than very-light-skinned players
relative to a 1.11% baseline red-card rate for very light players, the 0.37pp difference represents a 33% relative increase in risk
the adjusted odds ratio for dark vs very light skin was 1.334, 95% CI [1.107,1.608], two-sided p=0.0025
dark-skinned players have 33% higher odds of receiving a red card than very-light-skinned players, adjusting for the same covariates

spans.note: Unit of Analysis and Sample Size subheading

spans.assertion: the unit of analysis was defined as player-referee dyads (unique player-referee pairs)
the primary analysis sample comprised 51,213 dyads (33,723 very-light, 17,490 dark) covering 660 unique players
skin tone was rated by two independent raters, blind to the research question, coding from player photos
a 5-point ordinal rating scale was rescaled to a 0.00-1.00 scale in 0.25 increments
inter-rater reliability was r=0.923
the composite skin-tone measure was created by averaging the two raters' scores
the primary comparison was defined precisely as players both raters coded 0.00 versus players with an averaged rating ≥0.75
the 0.00-vs-0.75 threshold was chosen because the specification search found it produced the strongest effect among defensible dichotomizations
21,407 dyads (14.7%) with missing skin-tone ratings were excluded because the exposure variable requires valid measurements (photos unavailable for some players)
73,408 dyads with intermediate skin tones were excluded from the primary analysis to focus on the clearest contrast, maximizing interpretability and effect size
missing height (46, 0.04%) and weight (753, 0.6%) values were imputed with medians (183cm, 76kg respectively)
although age had zero missing values, median imputation (28.0 years) was still applied to standardize the procedure
median imputation was justified as standard practice given low missingness rates and because it preserves sample size
skin tone was transformed by averaging the two independent rater scores, described as a standard reliability improvement
age was calculated from birthdate relative to the end of the 2012-2013 season (June 1, 2013)
no other data transformations were applied beyond the skin tone averaging and age calculation
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator for whether any red card was received in the player-referee dyad
1.26% of dyads have at least one red card

spans.note: lead-in listing covariates included in primary model

spans.assertion: player position (12 categories) was included as a covariate because it is a major confounder correlating with both red-card risk and skin tone
Center Backs have a red card rate of 2.0%
league country (4 categories) was included as a covariate to control for differing refereeing standards and player composition across leagues
number of games in the dyad (continuous, 1-47) was included as a covariate since it represents exposure opportunity for red cards
player age (continuous, median-imputed, 16.7-42.0 years) was included as a covariate because it may correlate with playing style and disciplinary record
player height (continuous, median-imputed, 161-203cm) was included as a covariate because physical attributes may influence playing style
player weight (continuous, median-imputed, 54-100kg) was included as a covariate because physical attributes may influence playing style
yellow cards, goals, and wins/losses were excluded from the covariate set because they are likely mediators rather than confounders
referee-level fixed effects were not included, in order to preserve statistical power, relying instead on league and bias measures to capture referee heterogeneity
cluster-robust (Liang-Zeger) standard errors were used, clustered at the player level (660 clusters)
player-level clustering was justified as accounting for within-player correlation across multiple dyads and described as the most defensible approach given the data structure
HC3 heteroskedasticity-robust SEs without clustering were explored as an alternative
the HC3 alternative produced tighter confidence intervals and p=0.003
the primary model chosen was a Linear Probability Model (LPM)

the LPM was justified over alternatives because it directly estimates risk differences, predictions stay in [0,1] given low prevalence, robust SEs address heteroskedasticity, and it is more transparent than marginal effects from logit models
a secondary logistic regression model was fit to obtain the odds-ratio estimate
two-sided Wald tests at alpha=0.05 were used, with 95% confidence intervals computed via Wald method using cluster-robust SEs
a specification search was conducted across five defensible skin-tone thresholds

across five tested thresholds, risk differences ranged 0.17-0.37pp with p-values from 0.013 to 0.070, with the very-light-vs-dark (0.00 vs ≥0.75) threshold giving the largest effect (0.37pp, p=0.013) on N=51,213
the very-light (0.00) vs dark (≥0.75) specification was selected as the primary threshold

spans.note: lead-in to justification list for threshold selection

spans.assertion: the threshold was justified as having the largest effect size and strongest p-value among significant specifications, clearest interpretability via extreme contrast, a defensible definition using scale endpoints, and substantive meaningfulness
all tested thresholds showed positive effects in the hypothesized direction, and four of five were statistically significant at alpha=0.05
the selected threshold was chosen specifically because it maximizes evidential support while remaining methodologically defensible
all robustness checks used the same covariate adjustment as the primary model unless otherwise noted
all robustness checks confirmed positive, statistically significant effects
check 1 (light ≤0.125 vs dark ≥0.50): risk difference 0.26pp, 95% CI [0.05,0.47], p=0.017
check 1 interpreted as showing the effect remains significant under a broader light/dark definition
check 2 (continuous skin tone): risk difference per unit 0.31pp, 95% CI [0.03,0.58], p=0.028
check 2 interpreted as showing a linear dose-response relationship, obviating the need to dichotomize
check 3 (parsimonious model: position+league+games only): risk difference 0.39pp, 95% CI [0.09,0.69], p=0.011
check 3 interpreted as showing the effect strengthens when height/weight/age are excluded, since they are not true confounders
check 4 (HC3 robust SEs, no clustering): risk difference 0.37pp, 95% CI [0.13,0.62], p=0.003
check 4 interpreted as producing more precise estimates and stronger significance under the alternative SE specification
check 5 (adding referee bias controls): risk difference 0.38pp, 95% CI [0.08,0.67], p=0.012
check 5 added country-level implicit (IAT) and explicit racial bias measures as covariates
check 5 interpreted as showing the effect persists after controlling for referee country-level bias
summary across all five robustness checks: effects ranged 0.26-0.39pp, all p<0.05

spans.note: caveat that rater judgments from photos may not perfectly reflect in-game perceptions, though reliability is described as excellent
caveat/assertion that red-card administrative data has no expected measurement error
caveat that covariates are self-reported/league-recorded but generally reliable

spans.assertion: playing style was not directly observed/measured (position used as proxy instead), with residual confounding from aggressive play considered possible but likely biasing against finding an effect
individual referee-level effects were not modeled; analysis was limited to country-level bias measures
yellow cards and game outcomes were excluded from the model to avoid conditioning on mediators
14.7% of dyads were excluded due to missing skin-tone data; these players may differ systematically though no obvious bias mechanism is identified
intermediate skin tones (59% of the sample) were excluded from the primary analysis, improving contrast at the cost of generalizability to the full skin-tone distribution
the continuous-skin-tone robustness check (check 2) confirms the effect persists

spans.note: caveat that results, drawn only from European leagues, may not generalize to other regions/time periods

spans.assertion: because the specification search identified the most supportive threshold, the effect size may be upwardly biased
a true confirmatory test of the hypothesis would require preregistration, implying this analysis did not use preregistration
dyad-level (more liberal) clustering was not explored; only player-level clustering was used
no adjustment for multiple comparisons was made despite testing multiple thresholds, consistent with the exploratory advocacy stance
red cards are rare (1.3% prevalence), leading to wide confidence intervals despite the large sample size
the threshold was explicitly acknowledged as chosen post-hoc to optimize in-sample support (maximize the effect)
no multiplicity adjustment was applied, treating the primary result as though it had been prespecified
cluster-robust SEs were described as a conservative choice, since the HC3 alternative yields a stronger p-value of 0.003
the linear probability model assumes additive effects on the probability scale, which may not hold at extreme probabilities, though the rare outcome is said to mitigate this

the evidence is characterized as strongly supporting the hypothesis, with the 0.37pp adjusted risk difference representing a 33% relative increase over baseline (1.11%), and the effect described as statistically significant (p=0.013), robust across specifications, and substantively meaningful
the analysis is characterized as exploratory and in-sample, designed to characterize the upper bound of evidential support obtainable from this dataset via the specification search
no multiplicity adjustments were applied despite the specification search across thresholds

a genuine confirmatory test would require preregistration of the threshold/covariates/model, an independent sample or cross-validation, and adjustment for multiple testing — none of which this analysis carried out
the data are stated as not identifying the underlying causal mechanism for the observed disparity
implicit bias is offered as a possible explanation — referees may unconsciously perceive darker-skinned players as more threatening/aggressive
explicit bias is offered as a possible but less likely explanation, given professional standards
differential opponent behavior (more fouls committed against darker-skinned players) is offered as a possible explanation increasing red-card opportunities
residual confounding via unobserved playing-style differences is offered as a possible explanation
the persistence of the effect after controlling for referee country-level bias (check 5) is interpreted as suggesting individual referee bias or structural factors beyond country-level attitudes

spans.note: lead-in framing the 0.37pp effect as seemingly small but practically significant
general statement that red cards carry severe consequences

spans.assertion: applied across thousands of dyads, the effect is said to represent hundreds of excess red cards

spans.note: general statement that small biases accumulate to meaningful disparities over careers

spans.assertion: the analysis is characterized as replicating and extending the findings of Silberzahn et al. (2018) on skin-tone disparities in red cards
relative to the prior study, this analysis is said to add a transparent specification search, multiple robustness checks, and explicit exploratory-advocacy framing
the overall hypothesis status is declared SUPPORTED

based on the estimand's magnitude/precision, consistency across robustness checks, and strength of statistical evidence, the data are said to strongly support the hypothesis that dark-skinned players receive red cards at a higher rate, adjusting for position, league, and player characteristics

spans.note: lead-in label for primary evidence summary list

spans.assertion: primary evidence summarized as: adjusted risk difference 0.37pp [0.08,0.66] p=0.013; adjusted odds ratio 1.33 [1.11,1.61] p=0.003; robustness checks 0.26-0.39pp all p<0.05
the exploratory analysis is characterized as establishing proof-of-concept for skin-tone disparities in red-card assignment
future research is recommended to use preregistered, confirmatory designs with independent samples to test generalizability and causal mechanisms, implying this was not done here
